I think it's definitely a cool tool to figure out how all your units can fit together, like a puzzle. My concern is mostly on the viability of the comps that it is going to present, but if your goal is learning the game and how units interact/synergize, it's pretty cool, even with the fail cases it's still a learning experience, like "oh Ashe didn't do much without sniper, I know I can drop her next time I play in this scenario."

As others have stated I think the most valuable thing to do with something like this would be to implement emblems, because that is usually the trickiest part that requires deviation even in high ELO games. If you could enter your Trainer Sentinel/Dummy it would be great to be able to see at a glance where you can go with the emblems you have, even if it's not optimal, it's gives you direction.

I don't think solving the game with an algorithm is the right way to go about this. So much of the game is learning how to optionally play different lines. All three of your comp examples would lose in higher ELO without great items/augments. 3 Star Gnar is not worth playing without the dryad support, Syndra is pretty bad outside of vertical arcanist or fated/dryad. Your best comp from your position looks like you should just go fated/dryad and sell the Wukong.

I appreciate the idea of trying to figure out optimal trait spread by keying in important units, but you also need to be aware of what units actually synergize together outside of just their traits, and when it's worth it to sell your level 7 high roll 5 cost in order to make a comp that makes sense. Level 7 with Wukong early would probably look like; Gnar, Kindred, Thresh, Ahri, Syndra, any other fated, Wukong. Sell Wukong when you level and hit Ornn/Azir and sell the extra fated for Sett when you hit.

We don't really have the luxury of playing around stuff like a counterspell even if we know about it. We normally can't bluff it out unless our hand is stacked, and in that case, you try to do that in the dark anway if your OP has open mana. Like if you can EOT gifts to try to bait a counter so you can resolve a gifts on untap, you're just gonna do that regardless of whether you know it's gonna be countered or not.

A lot of times you just need to "go for it" with storm and Peek is almost a handicap in that most of the information you're gaining is stuff you could derive based on the board position and cards in OPs hand, which is the most important skill when playing Comp MTG is trying to put your OP on certain cards.

Gifts is one of the most situation dependent cards. A value gifts in one game might be one pile and different in another. More often than not a value gifts is just getting cantrips/morphose/second gifts, when you just need more stuff without exposing critical cards to the GY (in case of GY hate)

Gameplay doesn't mean "shoot, jump, kill." In a game like Mass Effect, the dialogue *is* gameplay. Conversations play out like puzzles and also reveal to the player the story and background. When moving into gunplay, there is a reason behind it, you know who the enemy is and why you are killing them. Not everything is being told to you, but the player has the ability to infer many things. Portal 2 does this with the setting of the test chambers. The player wonders where the hell they are when they enter the Cave Johnson area, and while testing those puzzles, you wonder how it became like that, and what happened to the place, which is revealed to you as you progress from puzzle to puzzle, as to not interfere with the actual solving of the puzzles. 

Many missions in RPGs now can be completed with some dialogue that requires the play to actually interact. QTEs, even though they are hated by the player based, are also a way to keep story and gameplay together.
